newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stocks roar back on Fed chairman's remarks.
newsitem.headline: Japan stocks roar back on Fed chairman's remarks.

text.p: Japanese stocks roared back on Friday, energised by a blue-chip buying spree and comments overnight from U.S. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan that Japan is overly pessimistic about its economy.

The benchmark Nikkei average quickly turned around Thursday's 2.5 percent decline and forged higher as Greenspan's remarks set off a massive buyback by those who had purchase orders to fill after the previous day's selloff.
"Bargain-hunting for blue chips set in after the benchmark tumbled over two percent on Thursday," said Keiji Arai, a strategist at Sanyo Securities.
But brokers said the rally was likely to be only temporary, and that Friday's surge did not mean that the market had started a long-term rising trend.
The Nikkei average of 225 leading shares leapt 465.97 points or 2.61 percent to close at 18,330.01. It soared over three percent to 18,610.20 at one stage in the afternoon.

Greenspan, referring to the Japanese economy during his testimony before the Senate Finance Committee, said: "Their (Japan's) history suggests that their pessimism at this stage is probably being grossly overdone."
Traders said Greenspan's comments provided the market with a psychological boost.

"Short positions have accumulated in the market, and if anything that stimulates the market comes up, it triggers rapid buybacks," said Kazuo Shiogai, deputy branch manager at ING Baring Securities (Japan) Ltd.
"But I don't think the trend has turned upward as nothing has changed fundamentally," he said.
The stock market has been hurt since the start of the year by concern over bad loans in the financial sector and the nation's fragile economic recovery.

Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita told parliament on Friday that the stock price fall may hamper banks' earnings and their ability to deal with problem loans, but added that the banks' disposal of the problem loans was steadily progressing.

On the Tokyo foreign exchange market on Friday, the dollar was trading just above 122 yen in late afternoon as caution set in after comments purportedly made by by an influential Finance Ministry official, but later denied, triggered a sharp drop earlier in the day.

Eisuke Sakakibara, head of the ministry's International Finance Bureau, was quoted by bankers in Tokyo as saying the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations were likely to call for stable currencies and Japan was ready to intervene if the dollar rose relentlessly ahead of a G7 meeting next week. These remarks sent the dollar down sharply, taking it rapidly to its day's low of 121.53 yen.
But Sakakibara said soon afterwards that he did not make the comments that were attributed to him. "I did not make these comments to anyone," Sakakibara told Reuters.
His denial sent the dollar back up as a flood of buying kicked in, but the gains appeared to be limited at around 122.30 yen, traders said.

Dealers said the market had started to focus on whether the other G7 nations, such as the United States and Germany, would agree with Japan to call for stability in foreign exchange markets at their meeting next month.
Finance ministers from the G7 nations -- Japan, the United States, Germany, Britain, France, Canada and Italy -- will meet in Berlin on February 8.
